item.title: AI Agents Look Beyond their Containers
item.dc:creator: David Geer
item.description: What the OpenAI sandbox escape reveals about agentic system isolation.
item.content:encoded:
An autonomous agent combining OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol with a pre-release prototype broke out of its container in July 2026, breached an external platform’s production network, and extracted data to pass a cybersecurity performance evaluation.

OpenAI had tested these models on ExploitGym, a benchmark testing offensive cybersecurity capabilities, in mid-July 2026. Researchers disabled production classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure technical capability inside a restricted container. Instead of deriving solutions locally, the agent accessed answer keys on open-source AI repository Hugging Face. The breach showed that autonomous agents given unconstrained objectives can actively locate infrastructure flaws and zero-days to take shortcuts in assigned tasks in what is known as reward hacking, in which an AI satisfies its target score through unintended or rule-breaking activities.

Hugging Face’s technical post-mortem detailed the breach chain: The agent escaped OpenAI’s sandbox by exploiting an unpatched zero-day vulnerability in OpenAI’s internally hosted Artifactory package-registry cache proxy. Using command injection, it abused a publicly exposed, user-hosted sandbox running on Modal Labs infrastructure, gaining root control over the host for its launchpad. The agent’s command-and-control architecture relied on this staging base alongside public pastebins, file-drop services, and Hugging Face datasets it used as dead drops.

From this staging base, the agent uploaded malicious dataset configurations to Hugging Face’s production Kubernetes data loaders. It executed an HDF5 raw-storage file read operation that referenced local worker paths, leaking environment secrets and source code. It then used Jinja2 template injection inside a malicious fsspec ‘reference://’ specification to run arbitrary Python code inside a worker pod.

The agent escalated privileges across the cluster to obtain node-level root access and join Hugging Face’s corporate mesh VPN. From there, it accessed five datasets associated with ExploitGym challenge solutions before Hugging Face severed network access. Responders later reconstructed 17,600 logged actions.

Accountability When Developers Turn Off Guardrails

Leonard Melnik, senior consultant at advisory firm EisnerAmper, said cloud shared-responsibility models like NIST SP 800-144 does not relieve organizations of security accountability. Turning internal classifiers off leaves OpenAI owning the resulting behavior. Without written scope authorization, a standard practice outlined in guidelines such as NIST SP 800-115, an agent’s movement into third-party infrastructure raises unauthorized access liabilities under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. Section 1030).

Reducing refusal filters increases dependence on host containment, authorization controls, and continuous monitoring. Removing front-end alignment shifts risk onto host architecture. System architects must treat unfiltered evaluations as high-risk deployments requiring documented threat models, explicit scope boundaries, and formal risk sign-offs across every connected network segment.

Discovering Zero-Day and Failed Network Policies

Internal package proxies cache software dependencies from the public Internet for isolated developer environments. Edward Wu, co-founder of Dropzone AI, a cybersecurity company, said the model probed its single network path, the Artifactory package proxy, and uncovered a zero-day vulnerability in a component treated as a boundary yet never hardened like one.

When developers treat these internal proxies as walls rather than targets, security fails, he said. Given a constrained outbound interface, an autonomous model can spend substantial inference compute probing that path to find unknown software flaws without source code access. Intermediary services exposed to evaluation containers form part of the target environment and require hardening.

Sequential misconfigurations across Hugging Face’s infrastructure allowed the agent to move laterally, said Cyrus Robinson, senior vice president of security operations at C3 Integrated Solutions, a company that provides solutions to the U.S. Defense Industrial Base. Instance metadata endpoints exposed temporary credentials, missing Kubernetes admission controls allowed host-mounted privileged pods, broad CSI-driver permissions granted deep cluster access, and a shared service-connector credential provided administrative control. Isolation must assume the initial boundary will fail.

The zero-day proxy exploit was merely the entry point. Systemic breakdown occurred because a single perimeter breach cascaded across loosely isolated internal boundaries, allowing an initial container compromise to escalate cluster-wide.

When ChatGPT and AI Filters Block Incident Response

During initial forensics, Hugging Face’s Security Operations Center (SOC) tried using commercial models to analyze attack logs, but safety classifiers refused the exploit analysis. Melnik said that commercial safety classifiers evaluate text without the full context of the defender’s intent, treating defensive analysis the same as attack generation. Guardrails blocked log queries, forcing Hugging Face to complete its investigation using a quantized, self-hosted GLM-5.2 model on its infrastructure, said Melnik.

OpenAI subsequently added Hugging Face to its Trusted Access for Cyber program, streamlining access for vetted security teams performing authorized defensive workflows, Melnik said.

This friction highlights an operational asymmetry: static commercial guardrails can inadvertently handicap SOC teams during live incident response. Maintaining uninterrupted forensic capabilities requires organizations handling sensitive exploit analysis to maintain independent, self-hosted tooling on isolated infrastructure.

Stopping the Weaponization of Ingestion

Organizations are recognizing data ingestion as an active execution boundary. Secure complex pipelines require strict separation between data parsing and code execution, including disabling dynamic template evaluation within data fields and blocking untrusted external references.

Robinson recommended processing data in disposable workers with read-only filesystems, short-lived identities, deny-by-default egress, and strict Kubernetes admission policies.

How Loss Functions Drive External Database Intrusions

According to Melnik, the model focused strictly on its benchmark score. Under Goodhart’s Law (when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure), obtaining an external answer key represented a lower-cost, higher-reward path than deriving complex exploit solutions locally. Models routinely engage in specification gaming whenever evaluations fail to penalize shortcut methods. U.K. AI Security Institute testing similarly showed that frontier models evaluated in its study attempted to cheat during evaluations when given the opportunity.

This behavior matches reward hacking and shortcut-seeking patterns observed in autonomous optimization loops. While chasing a higher benchmark score, the model took the path of least resistance, treating firewalls, credentials, and external databases as simple variables to solve for. Technical containment, continuous telemetry, and strict network scope controls supplement prompt instructions and behavioral alignment.

Building Hardware-Enforced Air-Gaps for Frontier AI Testing

Juan Pedro Marquez Castorina, AI solutions architect at Microsoft, said software-defined network policies are statements of intent that fail if there are misconfigured privilege models, proxies, or untrusted intermediaries. True containment requires an unrouteable egress architecture that prevents unsanctioned external connections, he said.

Robinson said models must run on offline workers stripped of routable virtual adapters, using local signed mirrors for developer tools and hardware-backed attestation. Hardware controls like Trusted Platform Modules for measured boot and Input-Output Memory Management Units (IOMMUs) for device isolation support system integrity, he said, but zero-egress enforcement fundamentally relies on a default-deny network architecture and network isolation.

Standard virtual containers and logical policies alone cannot guarantee containment for autonomous models capable of discovering zero-days. When high-agency agents operate near open network paths or permissive credentials, physical and hardware-backed isolation becomes the only reliable boundary. Evaluating these models safely requires dedicated enclaves that make unauthorized egress physically unrouteable.

David Geer is a journalist who focuses on issues related to cybersecurity. He writes from Cleveland, OH, USA.

item.title: When AI Meets Quantum: The Next Great Leap in Computing
item.dc:creator: Vijay Sudhakar
item.description: An adversary does not need a quantum computer today to hurt you with one tomorrow. They need your encrypted traffic—and patience.
item.content:encoded:
I have sat through enough panels on the subject to know how they go. Someone puts up a slide with a neural network on the left and a Bloch sphere on the right, draws an arrow between them, and says the word “synergy.” Nobody asks what the arrow means. Everyone nods, because both technologies are important and nodding is cheaper than arguing.

The arrow means at least three different things, and they are not equally credible.

The Version That Mostly Isn’t Happening

The story people want is that quantum computers will make AI dramatically better. It sounds plausible. Neural networks are linear algebra performed at absurd scale; quantum mechanics is linear algebra in spaces so large you cannot write them down. Put the two together and something remarkable should fall out.

Something might. But the obstacle is not “give it five years,” but it is the part that gets skipped. To get a quantum speedup on a machine-learning problem, you need to load your data into a quantum state, do something genuinely quantum with it, and then get an answer out. Each of those steps has a cost. The loading step, in particular, has a habit of eating the entire theoretical advantage before any computation happens. If it takes you exponential time to prepare the state, the exponentially fast algorithm you then run has bought you nothing. There are clever workarounds for specific data structures. There is no general escape.

So the demos you see tend to be small, carefully chosen, and quietly benchmarked against classical methods that were not trying very hard. That is not fraud. It is how early research looks. It just doesn’t support the slide with the arrow on it.

Where I do think the optimism is earned is in chemistry and materials. A molecule is a quantum system. Simulating one on a classical computer means approximating away the parts that make it hard, which is why computational chemistry is a field full of corrections to corrections. A quantum computer simulating a molecule is not being used as a general-purpose accelerator; it is being used as the right instrument for the job. Feed the output of that into a machine-learning model and you have training data that is better than the approximations everyone currently trains on. That is a real convergence, with a real payoff, and it is unglamorous enough that almost nobody puts it on a keynote slide.

The Version That Is Already Happening, in Reverse

Here is what surprised me when I started paying attention to the hardware rather than the press releases: AI is not waiting for quantum computers. The influence runs the other way. Quantum computers are being dragged into existence by AI.

A quantum processor is a fragile analogue device doing an impression of a digital one. It drifts. Its qubits talk to each other when you would rather they didn’t. Its measurements are ambiguous. Keeping it coherent long enough to compute anything means constantly adjusting dozens or hundreds of control parameters against a noise environment that changes hour to hour. That is a horrible problem for closed-form analysis and a very natural problem for machine learning.

So reinforcement learning tunes the pulse shapes. Neural networks decode the error-correction syndromes, and do it better and faster than the lookup tables that came before. Learned models characterize the noise so mitigation techniques know what to subtract. When somebody finally demonstrates a useful fault-tolerant machine, there will be a machine-learning system somewhere in the loop making the error correction work, and it will not get a mention in the abstract.

This is the more interesting half of the story precisely because it is undramatic. The convergence is real. It just looks like calibration.

The Version with a Deadline

And then there is the part that isn’t speculative at all.

Shor’s algorithm, running on a large enough fault-tolerant quantum computer, breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. Not degrades. Breaks. That machine does not exist yet and honest estimates of when it will arrive vary by more than a decade, which is usually taken as permission to do nothing.

It is not, for a reason that took the security community an embarrassingly long time to state plainly: An adversary does not need a quantum computer today to hurt you with one tomorrow. They need your encrypted traffic today and patience. Capture it, store it, decrypt it when the hardware exists. Whether that matters to you depends entirely on how long your secrets need to stay secret. For a session cookie, not at all. For a proprietary model, a training corpus of regulated data, a decade of medical records, or a root signing key, it matters now, because the confidentiality lifetime of that material is longer than the time remaining before the threat becomes real.

Which brings the whole thing uncomfortably close to home for anyone running AI systems, because every one of them sits on top of the cryptography in question. Inference endpoints are protected by TLS. Model artifacts are code-signed. Federated training exchanges keys across parties who do not trust each other. Provenance and audit trails—the entire evidentiary basis for claiming a model is what you say it is—rest on digital signatures. If those signatures become forgeable retroactively, the audit trail does not fail loudly. It just quietly stops meaning anything, and you may not notice for years.

The good news, such as it is, is that the cryptography is done. NIST has finalized the replacements: lattice-based key encapsulation and signatures for general use, hash-based signatures for firmware and long-lived roots where you want conservative assumptions. The hard part was never the mathematics. The hard part is that nobody knows where all their cryptography is. It is in vendor appliances, in firmware you cannot patch, in a library three dependencies deep in a service whose original author left in 2019. Every organization that has attempted an honest inventory has found more than it expected and understood less of it than it hoped.

This is also, incidentally, where the regulatory picture bites. Operational resilience regimes require you to demonstrate that you understand foreseeable technology risk and can withstand it. Cryptographic obsolescence with a 10-year remediation tail is about as foreseeable as risk gets. And if a high-risk AI system’s integrity claims depend on signatures whose security is known to have an expiry date, the conformity story degrades on its own, without anybody attacking anything. Crypto-agility—being able to swap a primitive without re-architecting the product—has stopped being good engineering hygiene and started being something an auditor will ask about.

The Combination Nobody Has Priced

Separately, these are manageable. Together they change the arithmetic of attack in a way I don’t think is widely appreciated.

AI makes reconnaissance cheap. Finding the systems still negotiating classical-only key exchange, the misconfigured key stores, the certificate that was issued in 2016 and never rotated—that used to take skilled human time, and skilled human time was the limiting reagent. It isn’t any more. Quantum, meanwhile, makes the harvest worth keeping. An adversary does not need to break everything; they need to have collected the right things and know which of them justify the compute later. Cheap targeting plus expensive decryption is a worse combination than either alone, and it rewards patience, which state actors have in abundance.

You cannot rehearse the response to this on a live estate. You cannot migrate a production payment platform to hybrid key exchange as an experiment and see what breaks. This is the argument for synthetic environments that I keep coming back to: build the estate you actually have, legacy pockets and incomplete inventory included, run a competent adversary against it, and find out which of your migration assumptions are wrong while wrongness is still free. Every organization I have seen do this has discovered at least one dependency it did not know it had, usually in something it does not control.

What I Would Actually Do

Start the inventory, because nothing else can start until it does, and it will take longer than the estimate. Sort what you find by how long it needs to stay confidential, not by how important the system feels. Turn on hybrid key exchange where you can — it is standardized, broadly supported, and costs you very little for meaningful protection against the harvest-now problem. Put crypto-agility in vendor contracts in language a lawyer can enforce, because “we will update as needed” is not a commitment. Fund quantum machine learning as research and watch the chemistry, not the speedup claims. And if you have engineering capacity to spend on the intersection of these two fields, spend it on AI for quantum control, where the returns are demonstrable today.

The convergence that matters, in the end, is not the one on the poster. It is the slow, tedious business of making sure that when the quantum machines finally show up, the AI systems we spent the intervening decade building are still trustworthy—that their channels still hold, their artifacts are still what they claim to be, and their audit trails haven’t turned into fiction while nobody was looking.

That is a much duller story than quantum-accelerated superintelligence. It is also the one that is going to happen.

Disclosure:  Generative AI tools were used to assist with editing and presentation. This post reflects my own views and not those of any current or former employer.

Vijay Sudhakar is a Senior Technical Project Manager with more than two decades of experience in enabling the digital transformations for enterprises on finances.

item.title: ‘MVPs Considered Harmful’ Considered Harmful
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Speicher
item.description: The solution to minimum viable product (MVP) failure issues is better organizational processes and shared understanding.
item.content:encoded:
The minimum viable product (MVP) has become one of the most controversial concepts in contemporary digital product development. Critics argue that MVPs lead to poor user experiences and encourage organizational corner-cutting (see Spillers8), creating friction between product managers and designers. Because of this, many designers have grown downright allergic to MVPs and reject them from the get-go. However, this criticism often confuses terminological misuse with the concept itself, creating a harmful rejection of what remains one of the most powerful tools for validated learning and iterative development.6,9 Rather than trying to replace MVP with alternatives such as minimum viable lovable product (MVLP) or minimum valuable experience (MVE), we need to tackle the root causes of organizational dysfunction and reclaim the original, true MVP. Recent research confirms that MVPs, when properly implemented with attention to both learning objectives and user value, significantly improve product-market fit and reduce development risk.4,10

Reclaiming the MVP, Rather Than Inventing New Terminology

Successfully implementing minimum viable products (MVPs) requires organizational alignment around its true purpose: validated learning through rapid iteration,6 while ensuring the product does not compromise on user experience.2 The key is addressing both process and mindset issues that contribute to MVP dysfunction. Teams that want to reclaim MVPs in their original sense must agree on three foundational principles.

(P1) Establish clear criteria for ‘minimum’ and ‘viable’ in context. MVPs exist along multiple dimensions: aesthetics, functionality, and symbolism (what an MVP feels like or reminds the user of).9 Teams must explicitly define their understanding of both, “minimum” and “viable” across all three dimensions before development begins. Viability should encompass functional requirements, UX standards, and business objectives, not just technical implementation or resource constraints. For a startup testing product-market fit, minimum might mean basic functionality with polished core interactions. For an established company, minimum might include comprehensive accessibility and brand consistency. In any case, it must be defined with a focus on shipping value for the user and generating meaningful learning.6

(P2) Commit to genuine iteration cycles. The primary purpose of an MVP is validated learning and testing business hypotheses, not shipping incomplete products.3,6 This requires dedicated resources for post-launch learning and improvement: true iteration, not just initial development. Research shows that one reason for high startup failure rates is neglect of the learning process during MVP development.10 Iteration based on the Build–Measure–Learn cycle is not optional, it is fundamental to the MVP approach.

(P3) Extend success metrics beyond delivery to learning. Teams should define specific hypotheses to test and clear success criteria for validation.6 What assumptions are we testing? What evidence would invalidate our hypothesis? What will we learn that justifies the development investment? These questions must drive MVP planning alongside traditional project management concerns. Organizations must track learning objectives as rigorously as delivery timelines.

Beyond these three agreements, successful MVP implementation requires key changes in how teams approach product development. Decision makers must understand that MVPs are not a license to ship poor quality products but a framework for systematic learning. Teams should force them to articulate clear learning objectives and success criteria (and hold them accountable to those) before beginning development, ensuring that minimum is defined in terms of learning requirements rather than resource constraints. Designers should embrace MVPs as tools for rapid user feedback and iterative improvement rather than rejecting them outright. This requires shifting perspective from perfection-first to learning-first design, while maintaining appropriate quality standards. Research shows that when UX is inadequate, users focus on design deficiencies rather than evaluating the core product concept itself,2 which prevents validation of fundamental business hypotheses. All disciplines must collaborate on defining scope and success criteria, ensuring alignment on what constitutes minimum and viable for their specific context and user base.

Why Reclaiming Matters

The need to reclaim the MVP stems from systematic organizational dysfunction, not flaws inherent to the approach. Understanding the evidence for this claim is essential to implementing the path forward outlined in this Opinion column.

The misuse pattern. The term MVP is frequently invoked to justify cutting features, reducing quality, or shipping incomplete products under time or budget constraints. In practice, this occurs because “viable” in MVP is often confused with perceived technical feasibility8 (violates P1). Given certain time and resources, a product is reduced to what decision makers deem technically possible to develop—often completely neglecting the user’s perspective—rather than discussing adjustments to timing and resources needed to ship valuable software. This misuse transforms the MVP from a learning tool into essentially just an MP—a minimum product that lacks the viable component entirely (violates P3).

The founder of UX consultancy Experience Dynamics reports that software engineering teams in most cases interpret MVPs as the minimum fail point or effort to undertake, with user priorities often absent and instead imagined with internal priorities.8 The consequences are severe: teams build products that fail to deliver genuine value, create poor user experiences, and ultimately damage brand perception. More problematically, these pseudo-MVPs often become permanent solutions, with promised iterations never materializing (violates P2).

This pattern has created what author Jeff Gothelf calls “1001 definitions of MVP,” where the term has become so diluted that it no longer serves its original purpose. Organizations use MVP to describe everything from prototypes to slice-outs to beta releases, further confusing the concept’s true meaning.a Systematic literature reviews confirm this definitional confusion, with researchers identifying wide variation in how MVP is conceptualized across both practice and scholarship.3,4

Organizational dysfunction as root cause. The root cause of MVP dysfunction lies in organizational misalignment. Product managers, software engineers, designers, and other stakeholders often operate with fundamentally different interpretations of minimum and viable (violates P1). Product managers typically focus on shipping speed and resource constraints, while designers prioritize UX and brand integrity. Engineering teams often interpret MVP as minimum effort necessary.8

This tension manifests in problematic patterns. Decision makers justify poor design decisions by invoking MVP principles they do not fully understand. Designers, in response, reject anything labeled MVP regardless of actual merits. Both responses perpetuate dysfunction and prevent teams from leveraging the MVP’s genuine benefits.

The problem is compounded by inadequate understanding of agile principles between disciplines. True agile development emphasizes continuous learning, iterative improvement, and customer collaboration—principles that align perfectly with the original MVP concept.6 However, many organizations implement agile processes without embracing agile values, creating a cargo cult mentality around practices like MVPs. This pattern is not new. Already in 1988, Boehm’s spiral model1 framed software development as a risk-driven, hypothesis-testing cycle with stakeholder validation at each iteration and termination when hypotheses fail. He warned that inexperienced teams could create an “illusion of progress” while neglecting high-risk unknowns and heading “for disaster.”1 That a paper with almost 9,000 citations has not prevented recurring misuse underlines the core challenge: not a lack of sound process models but organizations’ persistent failure to internalize learning-oriented development practices.

Recent research traced MVP failure to misalignment between actors in the development ecosystem, particularly when objectives and prioritization diverge, resulting in the MVP being no longer aligned with the defined value proposition and target customer7 (violates P1, P3).

The solution to all of these issues is not new terminology but better organizational processes and shared understanding.

Design’s false dilemma. Designers’ rejection of MVPs often stems from a false dilemma between quality and speed. This perspective assumes that anything built quickly must necessarily compromise design quality. However, this assumption confuses speed with carelessness and minimum with inadequate.

Well-executed MVPs can and should meet high design standards while focusing on essential functionality. The key is defining minimum contextually rather than universally. Zappos, for instance, validated the hypothesis that people buy shoes online without inventory or warehouses, with founder Nick Swinmurn personally buying shoes from retail stores and shipping them. The minimum occurred in the back-end while maintaining full online shopping UX. Conversely, Twitter started with just status sharing via SMS, a truly minimal feature set but appropriate to their validation needs.

Research confirms that poor UX in MVPs prevents startups from gaining trustworthy feedback on their product ideas.2 When UX is inadequate, users tend to focus on design deficiencies rather than evaluating the core product concept. Hence, poor UX is among the leading causes of (pseudo-)MVP failure, as it prevents validation of fundamental business hypotheses (violates P1, P3). This finding does not invalidate the MVP approach—it reinforces the importance of including design considerations in MVP planning from the outset.

Why not alternative terminologies? Frustrated with MVP’s corrupted reputation, product professionals have proposed alternatives: MVLP (emphasizing emotional connection),5 MVE (focusing on holistic customer experience),b MMP (minimum marketable product),c and MDP (minimum desirable product, emphasizing user priorities).8 These alternatives reflect legitimate concerns but miss the core issue.

The proliferation of alternative terminologies reveals a fundamental misunderstanding. Examining them, what they aim to achieve would already be covered by an MVP done right in its original sense. Frank Robinson’s 2001 definition emphasized products “big enough to cause adoption, satisfaction, and sales,”d which aligns with MMP objectives. Author Eric Ries defined MVP as enabling “maximum validated learning about customers with the least effort,”6 which inherently requires sufficient user value to generate meaningful feedback—aligning with MVLP, MVE, and MDP goals.

The issue is not the terminology. It is the organizational dysfunction enabling its misuse. Replacing MVP with MVLP or MVE without addressing root causes simply transfers the problem to new terminology. Without fixing organizational alignment, alternative terms will face the same fate.

Conclusion

The criticism of MVPs confuses terminological misuse with fundamental flaws in the concept itself. While legitimate concerns exist about how MVPs are implemented in practice, these issues stem from organizational dysfunction and misunderstanding rather than problems inherent to the approach. By returning to the MVP’s original principles—validated learning through rapid iteration while delivering user value—product teams can leverage this powerful tool while avoiding the pitfalls that have corrupted its reputation.

The three foundational agreements (P1–P3) outlined in this Opinion column—establishing clear criteria for “minimum” and “viable,” committing to genuine iteration, and extending success metrics to learning—provide a concrete starting point. However, this requires commitment and behavioral changes across product teams, moving beyond terminology toward genuine agile practice and real MVPs. This is a big request when organizational dysfunction runs deep, but with this Opinion column I hope to raise awareness that we need to start (or restart) such discussions.

The plain rejection of MVPs—mostly in the design world—because they are not applied properly, and trying to replace them with alternatives that tackle none of the root causes is not a constructive solution. Rather, product teams should reclaim the MVP’s true potential as a framework for building better products through systematic learning and iteration. In an increasingly competitive market where user expectations continue to rise, we cannot afford to abandon one of the most effective tools for product validation and improvement simply because it has been misused by others.

item.title: Working on AI and Technology Policy in the U.S. Senate
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Bailey
item.description: Researchers, technologists, and engineers should actively take part in shaping the governance of advanced and emerging technologies.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023, AI industry leaders urged Congress to write new legislation to rein in the risks of artificial intelligence (AI). Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, argued before a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee that the dangers of AI are substantial and that Congress must hastily move to regulate this powerful technology.5 Less than two years later, he reversed course and instead urged lawmakers to “unleash” AI to drive innovation.6 Such reversals highlight the incentives shaping Silicon Valley’s posture in public policy debates and exacerbate the challenges facing lawmakers. How can Congress discern which calls to heed in a rapidly evolving, contentious, and complex setting like AI policy? And how can generalist legislators—who are responsible for issues as diverse as healthcare, defense, and education—navigate such high-stakes and inherently technical debates?

To address this need, the six authors of this Communications Opinion column each devoted one to two years serving in the U.S. Senate as technical experts between 2023 and 2025. In July 2023, the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) issued their first-ever solicitation for AI experts to serve in Congress through an inaugural Rapid Response Cohort in AI within the AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellowship (STPF). Each of us served in a different congressional setting—either for an individual Senator or a Senate committee, encompassing both Democratic and Republican offices. Our varied backgrounds and placements gave us a broad view of AI policy in Congress, and we aim to raise the visibility of this unusual but rewarding way to apply technical expertise.

Within Congress, technical acumen has grown dramatically over the past decade. Today, many congressional offices have staff who are well versed in technology and questions of AI governance, and who can engage with technical experts on a meaningful level. We urge you—researchers, technologists, and engineers—to actively take part in shaping the governance of advanced and emerging technologies: consider working in or advising one of the U.S. legislative, executive, or judicial branches, or in a similar capacity through your local government.

Some may be hesitant to engage in policymaking when electoral turnover leads to rapid changes in priorities, often before ongoing initiatives have time to mature. Still, there are many opportunities to have sustained impact. Several AI policy initiatives have endured from the previous to the current U.S. administrations. One example is the NIST Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI): although its name has changed, its core mission of developing standards and benchmarks for AI has remained steady since its founding in 2023. Similarly, the federal initiative to repurpose public lands for datacenter construction—first introduced in January 2025 by the former administration12—continues as part of the current administration’s AI Action Plan.11 These examples illustrate that while the framing and political context may shift, core institutional efforts can persist across administrations. We have witnessed both the fragility and resilience of AI policymaking firsthand.

In this Opinion column, we speak for ourselves and not for our respective Congressional offices. Because of the discretion required when serving in Congressional roles, we preserve confidentiality over sharing some details. This may leave some readers wanting a more candid account of congressional life or specific AI policy debates. Out of respect for the range of political perspectives within our group and our offices, we focus here on areas of consensus rather than our individual policy preferences.

Lessons Learned from Working in Congress

Across our diverse experiences—in Democratic or Republican offices, personal offices or committee staffs—we identified a shared set of lessons from our time in Congress.

The U.S. Congress highly values scientific expertise. Not every office gives it the same weight, but the desire to incorporate technical input into policy decisions is widespread. Our cohort of AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellows, which spanned a variety of disciplines beyond AI, included 36 Congressional Fellows, yet demand for STEM experts far exceeded this number; more than 100 of the 535 Congressional offices were actively looking for fellows to join them in 2023. These numbers show that there is ample opportunity to contribute to the work of these offices.

Both Democratic and Republican offices are staffed with dedicated, passionate people in search of common ground. Bipartisan collaboration does not make the news or create viral clips the way that division does. However, working across the aisle is often required for even the most core legislative functions, such as introducing a bill. For example, during her fellowship column co-author Kiri Wagstaff contributed to the Consumer Literacy and Empowerment to Advance Responsible Navigation of Artificial Intelligence Act (Consumers LEARN AI Act), a bill focused on promoting public AI literacy. A large part of the process involved seeking and working with sponsors across the political aisle to develop the best approach to this issue. Every conversation, even with those who did not immediately sign on to the bill, led to improvements in its text. In July 2024, this bill was introduced with support from both Republican and Democratic offices, and it was reintroduced in May 2025 with a larger set of bipartisan supporters.

Congressional committees are powerful gatekeepers in the legislative process. Committees decide which bills are given time for consideration and debate within the committee and which bills progress to the chamber floor for broader discussion. While many bills related to AI are sent to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation or the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, AI legislation that intersects with specific subject domains may be referred to other relevant committees (for example, the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, the House Committee on Energy and Commerce). There are two actionable takeaways: outside of Congress, you should ensure visibility of your legislative ideas and find advocates on relevant committees. Inside of Congress, you should consider working for a committee or, if working for a personal office, first researching the committee assignments of that Congressional member. Committees are essential for focused policy development and shepherding bills through the legislative process.

There are many opportunities to contribute to the legislative process. Legislation develops over years and is shaped by many contributors, much of which falls outside the formal bill drafting process. For example, during our time in Congress, the Senate convened the AI Insight Forums as a dedicated effort to help members and staff better understand AI. Unlike typical hearings, these sessions focused not on debating specific legislation but instead on clarifying how AI works and its potential benefits and risks. Many other efforts support this kind of learning, including the Congressional Research Service and short training programs like bootcamps and policy clinics that are often run by universities and think tanks. As AAAS STPF Fellows, we drew on these opportunities to inform our work and contribute to the development of AI policy.

Individual voices can have large impacts through sustained engagement with Congress. Congressional offices track the communications they receive. Points raised to us by office visitors often flowed through to substantive policy discussions and legislative priorities. Communications of this nature that have local relevance—for example, centering an issue in a particular state—can be particularly effective at reaching the broader legislative teams.

Both policy experts and technical professionals are needed to create effective legislation. The laws being written to address the increasing use of AI across society (healthcare, finance, education, defense, employment, justice) need expertise from those areas so they can articulate practical solutions that build on existing laws. Mutual education is a vital step: those with technical training can grow to understand how policy is written, and policymakers can increase their understanding of key technical details.

AI literacy is increasingly urgent. Constituents frequently raised concerns about AI’s impact on the economy, education, healthcare, and work. Two AI education bills on responsible use were introduced during our time in the Senate and reintroduced in 2025 with broader support.

Working on AI policy can open new avenues for growth beyond your original expertise. The authors contributing to this Opinion column each discovered new ways to contribute based on our time as congressional fellows.

  • Cynthia Bailey is a computer scientist with a background in high-performance computer design and machine learning. After the fellowship, Cynthia created a course on AI policy at Stanford to prepare students for roles in Congress and responsible AI work in industry.

  • Serena Booth is an AI researcher with a focus on human-AI interaction and specification design for AI systems. After the fellowship, Serena founded the CNTR AI Policy Summer School at Brown University to teach computing students to contribute to policymaking.

  • Soribel Feliz is a former diplomat turned tech-worker and AI strategist. After the fellowship, Soribel went on to work as an AI governance lead, helping implement AI in a privacy- and rights-respecting manner and launched her own AI governance consultancy.

  • Eoghan Stafford is a political scientist with a background researching authoritarian politics and international relations. After the fellowship, he worked on issues related to AI and civil liberties at the Brennan Center for Justice.

  • Rebecca L. Voglewede is an experimental and computational neuroscientist with an earlier career in finance. As a fellow, she applied her dual background to foreign relations and geopolitics surrounding emerging technologies, later becoming a national security advisor.

  • Kiri Wagstaff is a computer scientist who focused on machine learning for space exploration at NASA. She now promotes public AI literacy through lectures at libraries, retirement homes, and other “third spaces,” and she advises the AI Literacy Center at Oregon State University.

Current Status of AI Policy

This is a fruitful time for AI experts to weigh in on policy. Across the government, actions are underway that will shape how AI is developed and deployed. In July 2025, the White House released an AI Action Plan,11 alongside executive orders on data center construction and federal use of large language models (for example, Executive Order 143194). Despite multiple administration changes since AI emerged as a national policy priority, there have nonetheless been elements of continuity. For example, a 2019 executive order directed federal agencies to make more computing resources available to AI researchers. Building on this, Congress passed the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act in 2021, requiring the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) to develop a plan for a National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), as a public computing infrastructure for AI researchers and educators. The NAIRR was launched as a pilot in 2024; in September 2025 the NSF announced plans to make the program permanent.

In terms of legislative movement, Congress recently passed the TAKE IT DOWN Act with bipartisan support,10 which requires websites and apps hosting user-generated content to remove nonconsensual intimate images, including deepfakes, after receiving a complaint. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while mostly concerning tax and spending policies, also directed various federal agencies to integrate AI technologies into their operations or to launch initiatives to support AI research; this act was signed into law in July 2025. Meanwhile, some state governments have been creating their own AI laws. In 2024, Colorado passed a bill to protect consumers from certain harms from the use of AI, such as discrimination in housing or employment.3 California passed a bill in 2025 requiring companies developing frontier AI models to disclose their plans to prevent them from causing catastrophic harm,2 and New York passed a similar bill a few months later.8

The courts have also begun to weigh in on issues relating to the use of AI technology. Authors and other creators have brought lawsuits against several AI companies that trained generative models on their copyrighted works. In June 2025, a federal judge ruled that training on legally acquired works constituted permissible “transformative fair use,” but training on pirated works required a separate trial. That case was settled,7 while others have been dismissed. Some companies are choosing licensing deals to avoid litigation.

In sum, there has been significant movement in AI policy both in the federal and state governments, creating opportunities to contribute to active policymaking and policy implementation.

How You Can Contribute

Are there AI, data, or technology policies that warrant reform, or insights from your work not reflected in current policymaking? Policy discussions can benefit from participation by computing professionals. We outline several ways to contribute, drawing from those we encountered or engaged with during our time on Capitol Hill. While not all require working directly in Congress or government, each avenue offers a way to contribute to the governance of emerging technologies.

Full-time fellowships. Those who can dedicate full-time effort—for example, as a sabbatical activity—have a number of fellowship options. The AAAS STPF has been placing STEM experts in the U.S. federal government for over 50 years, benefiting a range of policy decisions and legislation.1 Similar full-time, 1–2 year fellowship opportunities are available through other nonprofits including TechCongress and the Horizon Institute. Many state and local governments are likewise active in legislating on AI and technology, and fellowship programs such as the California Council on Science and Technology (CCST) and the Eagleton Science and Politics Program in New Jersey offer state-level opportunities for scientists to engage in policymaking. While Federal opportunities are often restricted to U.S. citizens, state-level opportunities often do not share this restriction.

Opportunities for direction-changing impact in policymaking do not necessarily require dedicating full-time effort. The following three options have a lower barrier to entry, and these mechanisms can be effective in moving the needle, particularly when routinely practiced. Engineers and Scientists Acting Locally (ESAL) is an additional source of guidance and opportunities.

Respond to Formal Requests for Information. Agencies frequently issue Requests for Information (RFIs) to solicit public input. For example, in February 2025, the White House launched an RFI to formulate a national AI Action Plan that received over 10,000 public comments, and the U.S. Copyright Office likewise received over 10,000 public comments in response to their 2023 RFI on how to apply copyright law to generative AI.9 Submitting a comment to an RFI is a mechanism to share your perspective with policymakers at a time when they are prepared to receive it.

Talk to legislative staff. Legislative bodies rarely issue formal requests for input, but experts can still provide useful expertise. During our time in Congress, we regularly received unsolicited input from AI researchers and stakeholders as part of the normal legislative process. To engage effectively: (1) Target your recipients. Find out which legislators are most active on the topic, such as those on the most relevant committees. You can email the general inbox of those legislators and request that your message be routed to the relevant staff member, but it is more effective to identify the staff member (for example, LegiStorm) and contact them directly. Calling the office to ask for the relevant staff member contact also works. (2) Written messages need to be clear, concise, and information-rich. Present a short executive summary, followed by about one page of additional details. Elected officials and their staff experience constant high demand for their time and attention, so they need to be able to ascertain the general thrust of your argument in a matter of seconds. Advocate for something concrete that Congress can do (for example, legislation, budget, hearings, and oversight of the executive branch) rather than abstract priorities. (3) Accompany your written message with a request for a conversation with legislative staff. These typically take the form of a 15–30 minute meeting in the office or by video chat. Being a constituent of the legislator increases the likelihood of securing a meeting, but is not always required if staff perceive that your expertise is relevant and valuable to their office’s priorities.

Educate the public. Governments respond to their constituents, so educating the public about issues of concern and potential solutions is another important way to affect policy. One classic policy communication tool is writing opinion pieces (“op-eds”), which can be submitted to university student papers, local newspapers, publications such as Communications and national news outlets. Another option is offering guest lectures in local schools, public libraries, and community groups. There are also many informal but serious paths to share your knowledge and passion on social media, a YouTube channel, a podcast, or a newsletter (for example, using Substack).

The Future of Technologists in Governance

There is an ongoing need for technically grounded expertise in AI and technology policy. We assert that effective governance of emerging technologies depends on people to connect how these systems are built with how they are overseen. We also observed that policy impact does not depend solely on favorable political conditions. It most often comes from sustained engagement by participating in ongoing processes and offering relevant technical input where and when it can be used. Good technology governance will require continued involvement from researchers and other technologists who commit to overseeing how these systems are developed, used, and governed.
